transcript.text: Zanussi dishwasher keeps tripping the electrics, not every time though. Usually about 15 mins in. Model ZDT21006FA

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. Please leave it unplugged now. It mustn't be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it, because something in it is leaking current to earth. The timing is a useful clue. About 15 minutes in is usually when a dishwasher has filled, is circulating and is heating the water. 1. Heater element (or flow-through heater) leaking to earth. This is the classic cause. 2. Circulation pump or its wiring breaking down. It runs at the same stage, so it's the main alternative.
3. Less likely: water getting into the base onto wiring, a damaged mains lead or plug, or a chafed wire in the door loom. 1. Look along the mains lead and plug for cuts, crushing or scorch marks, and check the socket. Any damage there points to the lead or supply rather than the internals. If you see burning, keep it isolated.
2. Pull it forward slightly, with towels down, and look and feel for water underneath or around the base. Wetness suggests a leak reaching the electrics, and the engineer will need to find that too.
3. Think back over the times it tripped. If it happens mainly on hot programmes, that points strongly at the heater. If it trips on cool or quick washes too, the pump becomes more likely. If it ever tripped the moment you opened or closed the door, mention that, as it suggests the door wiring. If nothing obvious turns up, which is normal, an engineer can insulation-test the heater and pump to pin it down. A heater element is usually a reasonable repair on a machine like this. Don't keep resetting the trip and re-running it to test the theory. Can you tell me the answer to point 3, and whether it's the RCD (the switch with a test button) that drops rather than a single breaker?

It's mostly on the 65C programme, usually 10-20 mins in. The quick cold rinse has never tripped it. And yes, it's the RCD in the consumer unit that goes, a whole bank of circuits including the fridge goes off with it. It's not a single breaker.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
That pattern points quite firmly at the heater. An RCD trips when current leaks to earth rather than from simple overload. It happens mostly on the 65°C programme, 10 to 20 minutes in, which is when the machine is heating hard, and never on the cold rinse. That's good evidence against them. The classic fault is a heater whose insulation breaks down once it gets hot, which is also why it doesn't happen every time. 1. Heater element, or flow-through heater assembly, leaking to earth. This is the strong favourite. Depending on the design, the heater is either a separate element or built into the pump housing. An engineer will confirm which and insulation-test it.
2. A small leak that only appears on hot washes, dripping onto wiring in the base. This is less likely, but the base check below would show it.
3. The circulation pump or its wiring. This is unlikely, given the cold rinse never trips it. I'm fairly confident it's the heater, but only an insulation test proves it. It still mustn't be used until an engineer has checked it. A heater fault is usually a worthwhile repair on a dishwasher like this, so it's worth getting it looked at rather than writing it off. After each trip, check the fridge has come back on and keep its door shut while it's off. Leaving the dishwasher unplugged also protects the fridge. One more thing before you book someone. With it unplugged, did you spot any water under or around the base, or any damage or scorching on the plug or lead? Water underneath would mean the engineer needs to find a leak as well as test the heater.
The floor under it is dry and the socket is dry too. No visible leak or damage that I can see, and no burning smell either.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
That helps. A sound plug and lead and no burning smell, the simpler outside causes are much less likely. That leaves the heater as the clear favourite. 1. Heater or flow-through heater assembly leaking to earth once it gets hot. This fits everything: the RCD drops, it happens mostly on the 65°C programme 10 to 20 minutes in, and it never happens on the cold rinse.
2. A small internal leak dripping onto wiring. A dry floor makes this less likely, but it doesn't rule it out. Many dishwashers have a base tray that catches internal drips before they reach the floor, so the engineer should glance in there too.
3. The circulation pump or its wiring. This is unlikely, because it runs on the cold rinse without tripping. There's nothing more useful you can safely check yourself. Proving it needs an insulation test on the heater and pump, and that's an engineer's job. It still mustn't be used until an engineer has checked it. That points them straight at the heating circuit. On many modern dishwashers the heater is built into the pump housing rather than being a separate element, so they'll confirm which type yours has. A heater fault is normally a worthwhile repair, unless the machine is quite old or has other problems. How old is it roughly, and is it still under any warranty or extended cover? If it's covered, contact the manufacturer or your cover provider rather than paying for a call-out yourself.
It's about 8 years old. I don't know about any warranty or extended cover, so I'm not sure.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
At about 8 years old it's usually still worth repairing. Most dishwashers last around 10 to 12 years, and a heater fault is a single repair rather than a sign the whole machine is wearing out. It mustn't be used until an engineer has checked it, so here's how to decide and check cover. Repair or replace:
1. If it otherwise washes well, doesn't leak and has no rust in the tub or worn racks, repair is normally the better value.
2. Ask the engineer for a fixed quote covering diagnosis, part and labour. Get it before they start work. The repair may need the full pump-and-heater assembly rather than a separate element, and that costs more.
3. A rough rule: if the quote comes to more than about half the price of a comparable new dishwasher, or other problems turn up, replacing it starts to make more sense. Worth checking for cover before you pay for a call-out:
1. Look for purchase paperwork or an extended warranty letter. Check any appliance or breakdown plan in your bank statements.
2. Check your home insurance policy for appliance or accidental breakdown cover. Some packaged bank accounts include it too.
3. Contact the retailer if you bought it on finance or with an added care plan. If none of that turns anything up, an independent appliance engineer or Zanussi's own service is the next step. Tell them it trips the RCD mostly on the 65°C programme, 10 to 20 minutes in, and never on a cold rinse. That points them straight at insulation-testing the heating circuit.
